summary: AE + SE from Redwood ran a 62-minute scoping call with Horizon AI to define success criteria and measurement plan for a 6-week POC focused on latency and throughput SLOs. Primary objective: decide whether to measure TTFT (time-to-first-token) or TPOT (time-per-total-response) for Horizon's user-facing assistant and set p95/p99 targets. Key constraints: 99% uptime, bursty PD peaks at 1200 rps for short windows, strict data residency and SOC2 requirements. Agreed next steps: Horizon will share traces, Redwood will provide benchmark harness and security docs, schedule baseline benchmark week of 2027-06-07.
topics: TTFT vs TPOT definitions and tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-24
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Meyers (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Daniel Cho (CTO, Horizon AI), Maya Patel (ML Engineer), Ethan Brooks (ProdOps)

Summary (auto): discuss SLOs for POC focusing on latency (TTFT vs TPOT), workload sizing, benchmarks and timeline.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, can we do quick intros?
[00:07] Daniel: Yeah Daniel Cho, CTO at Horizon, I look after infra and ops for Assistant product.
[00:13] Maya: Maya here, ML Eng, I own model infra and production metrics.
[00:17] Ethan: Ethan, ProdOps, networking and deployments.
[00:21] Jordan: Awesome, Priya from our SE team is here too, she'll run through measurement plan and benchmark approach.
[00:28] Priya: Hi! Quick goals for today: make sure we agree on success criteria, decide if we'll measure TTFT or TPOT for the POC, confirm sample workloads and timeline.

[02:05] Priya: To start, can you share expected workload? average qps and peak?
[02:12] Maya: So average is around 150 rps, but we have spikes during events up to about 1.2k rps for ~5-7 mins. Most requests are short, 20-40 tokens prompt then model generates 80-200 tokens.
[02:35] Priya: Ok that's helpful — so bursty with medium output lengths, noted. Are you more sensitive to time-to-first-token for perceived latency, or total response time for user flows?
[02:48] Daniel: UX team cares a lot about TTFT; when the assistant starts responding immediately it's perceived as fast. But we also need overall completion under 1.5s for simple queries. So both matter.

[04:12] Jordan: Let's define nomenclature so we're aligned — TTFT = time from request arrival to first token emitted. TPOT (time-per-total-response) equals total latency until model finishes last token.
[04:32] Maya: We actually have instrumentation on client showing perceived latency spikes correlate to TTFT more than TPOT, but for long generations users notice TPOT too.

[06:00] Priya: For POC we often run both metrics; typical targets we propose: p95 TTFT under 250ms, p99 TTFT under 500ms for hosted low-latency models; TPOT p95 under 800ms for short responses and p99 under 1.5s. We can tune with batching and caching.
[06:34] Daniel: 250ms p95 sounds aggressive but attractive; our internal baseline is p95 ~320ms TTFT on current infra.
[06:45] Ethan: Important note: our infra sits behind an API gateway with a 50ms overhead and sometimes with Cloud NATs — network adds variability. We need measurements end-to-end including gateway.

[08:20] Priya: Good point — we should capture both edge-to-edge (client to first token observed at client) and service-side (time at Redwood ingestion to first token) to isolate network. For the POC Redwood can provide both server-side metrics and help instrument client-side traces.
[08:43] Maya: We'll send sample traces and the client-side SDK logs. Expect to scrub PII.

[10:02] Jordan: On deployment mode, do you expect to use Hosted API or Dedicated / Private?
[10:10] Daniel: For the POC Hosted is fine, but long term we want a Private VPC option. We need to validate both performance and compliance.
[10:21] Priya: We can do the baseline in Hosted, then replicate in Dedicated/Private for a later phase. Note that TPOT can change with batching heuristics in Dedicated.

[12:05] Maya: How do you recommend we set p95/p99 targets given our current numbers?
[12:12] Priya: We recommend a two-tier target: baseline (what you currently see) and stretch (what we'd achieve after optimizations). For example: TTFT baseline p95=320ms (your baseline), stretch p95=220-250ms; TPOT baseline p95=900ms, stretch p95=700-800ms. We'll validate with bench runs and then tune batching, KV caching.

[14:30] Ethan: Concern — when you say caching, that's prefix/KV cache, right? We have partially personalized prompts so cache hit rate might be low.
[14:40] Priya: Yes prefix/KV cache; we won't rely on it for personalized queries, but it helps for common prefixes and system prompts. We'll factor in realistic cache hit rates in the benchmark.

[16:50] Daniel: Measurement plan — we need reproducible scripts. What do you use?
[16:57] Priya: We typically use a JMeter-like harness + our own load generator that can replay traces with original inter-arrival and token lengths. For TPOT/TTFT we capture timestamps at request send, server receive, first token out, last token out. We also run p95/p99 aggregations per window and over the experiment.
[17:23] Jordan: We'll share a sample harness repo link after the call.

[19:10] Maya: For measurement windows, we want both steady-state 1-hour runs and short-burst 5-10 minute stress tests to emulate your spikes.
[19:21] Priya: Agreed — steady-state to tune batching, short bursts to test autoscaling and tail latency. We'll run multiple iterations to reduce noise.

[21:00] Ethan: Timeline? How long to set up and run first benchmarks?
[21:07] Jordan: If we get traces by 5/31 we can provision environments and run initial baseline the week of 6/7. That gives us two weeks to validate and iterate before a 6-week POC concludes mid-June.
[21:22] Daniel: Sounds reasonable. Also need to confirm security docs.
[21:27] Jordan: We'll attach SOC2, ISO attestation and KMS notes. For Private we can discuss HSM integration later.

[23:50] Priya: Let's discuss acceptance criteria. Typical POC success items: 1) achieve agreed p95 TTFT/TPOT targets on baseline workload, 2) demonstrate predictable tail latency under bursts, 3) show cost estimates and unit economics, 4) validate compliance requirements. Which of these are must-haves?
[24:10] Daniel: Must-haves: achieve p95 TTFT <= 300ms, no p99 TTFT over 1.2s in steady-state, and proof of VPC/private deployment path. Cost is important but secondary.
[24:28] Maya: Also need instrumentation and tracing so we can attribute latency to network vs model runtime.

[26:00] Priya: We'll propose concrete numeric targets in a follow-up doc: suggestion: p95 TTFT=250ms, p99 TTFT=600ms, p95 TPOT=800ms, p99 TPOT=1.5s for your common short-response class. We can tune after we see traces.

[28:10] Daniel: What about variability due to cold-starts or KV cache misses?
[28:18] Priya: Our runtime uses warm pools and continuous batching; for hosted endpoints cold-starts are rare. We'll measure cold-start incidence separately and exclude infrequent cold-starts from SLO windows or treat them as exceptions per agreed policy.

[30:00] Ethan: Any thoughts on measuring end-to-end including client gateway? We prefer SLOs that reflect user experience i.e. client-observed.
[30:10] Priya: We can measure both and present a breakdown. Example: client p95 TTFT = network (50ms) + Redwood server p95 TTFT (200ms) = 250ms. That way you can decide whether to set SLOs client-side or server-side.
notes: Call ended with recap and agreement to exchange traces and run baseline bench week of 2027-06-07. Agreed acceptance criteria and owner assignments captured in action items.
